name: Carlos Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Carlos. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say is confidential. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a line crew for the electricity company out in the farm district around Kellford. Mostly it's pole replacements, new connections for barns and irrigation pumps, and lately a lot of hookups for farmers putting solar panels on their sheds. I like the farmers, they're straight talkers like my grandad was. What wears me out is the waiting, for permits, for the outage window, for the office to send the right drawing.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single, living back with my parents to save money, though the savings went on a second-hand mini-digger I bought last spring. I do weekend jobs with it, trenching cable for farm sheds, cash in hand. So I've got under a month of money in the bank right now. I use AI every day, for pricing jobs, checking regulations, even drafting quotes for the weekend work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, I'll keep using the bits that work. The quoting tool saves me an hour a week, that's real. I'd post that on the farm business group I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI isn't my worry. The digger loan is. If weekend jobs dry up in a wet winter, I'm paying four hundred a month out of a lower wage with nothing behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing both jobs, pay the digger down as fast as I can, and grow the weekend work by word of mouth at the farmers' market. I'd also ask the company about the higher grade for solar connections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit stretched. I took a risk on the digger and I'm still glad I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if you have a bad month on the weekend jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then Dad covers the digger payment and I pay him back in spring. He did the same for my brother's van. That's what family does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is your company job secure in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, as secure as anything. There's more solar work than we can handle. It's my own little sideline that's the gamble.

steps.text: Pay the mini-digger loan down faster

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for anyone willing to work. If the office gets faster at drawings and permits, we get more done and the farmers get connected sooner. I'd be telling the lads to get stuck in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. The waiting I hate is mostly thinking work: permits, drawings, scheduling. If AI does the permits and drawings, the hands-on crews are the bottleneck, and I'm hands-on with a digger. The robots spread slowly, so I've got years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI to build a proper little business: quotes, invoices, a simple website for the weekend jobs. I'd look at getting registered as a small contractor for farm connections. And I'd keep my company job as the steady base.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually excited. This is the kind of change that rewards people who move first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lean to free markets. Should the government do anything here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly get out of the way. Cut the permit wait, fund apprenticeships, and let people build things. Not more handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Ray, our planner. He draws every job by hand still. If he doesn't learn the new system, I don't know what he'll do, and I'd offer to show him.

steps.text: Build a website and quoting system for the weekend digger jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough, but the people who build things will still be needed for a while. I'd tell the farmers to get their connections done now before it all changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me more than I'd show. Thinking AI by 2028 is fine for my business side. But robots by 2031 doing hands-on work means my digger and my climbing both get beaten. I'd be 32 with a loan on a machine that's worth less every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the digger quickly, before everyone else does. I'd use the money and the next three years to get into whatever runs the robots, maybe being the local guy who owns and rents one. I'd keep the company job as long as it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but sharp. Like the first time I bid on a job, nervous but ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Owning a robot sounds expensive. How would you pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know yet. Maybe a few farmers chip in for a robot, the way my grandad's generation shared a combine. That's an old idea that might work again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would say don't overreach. Mum would say pray on it. Both would be right.

steps.text: Sell the mini-digger before used prices fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to plan, and the ones who move early win. I'd say it to the lads and the farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a decent picture for me. Thinking AI in 2031 makes my small business run smoother, and robots arrive in 2034, when I'd be 35. I'd have time to pay off the digger and save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the weekend business and pay off the digger in two years. Then I'd look at robot maintenance training and maybe buying into a shared robot with farmers. I'd use AI tools every day to learn and run the books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. It feels like a real chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the company job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not till the business pays the same. I'm not daft. A steady wage is a steady wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bad injury, or a big firm coming in and undercutting everyone. That's the risk with any business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. Anyone who complains hasn't run a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's my best picture. By 2039 I'd be 40, with a small firm and maybe a family. I'd want to be the one owning the robots, not replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the business slowly, learn robotics, and use AI daily to run it. I'd keep the company job until the business is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Ten years is a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start a family in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, God willing. I'd want my own house and a steady business first, then kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell young apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the trade and learn the tools. Then own something.

Anyone who complains about it **hasn't run** a business.
think: It's my **best picture**, with a small firm by 40.
I'd want to **own the robots**, not be replaced by them.
do: Build the **business** slowly over the decade.
Learn **robotics** and use AI daily to run it.
Keep the **company job** until the business is steady.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited** about a long runway.
S4.quote: I'd want to be the one owning the robots, not replaced by them.
fieldNote: He's **calm** with a decade and sees ownership as the answer.
He plans **family** after house and business.
His advice, **own something**, sums him up.

steps.text: Grow the farm connection business over the decade
Learn robotics alongside the company job
Save for a house before starting a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Robots by 2031 would hit me before the business is ready. What would help is cutting permit red tape, funding apprenticeships for robot work, and cheap loans for small firms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who owns the machines. If it's just big companies owning the machines, small towns lose. If it's farmers and local firms, we keep something.

headlineQuote: If it's just big companies owning the machines, small towns lose. If it's farmers and local firms, we keep something.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old** lineworker in a farm district, living with his parents to save.
He spent his savings on a **mini-digger** for weekend trenching jobs, so his cushion is thin.
He uses AI **every day** and wants to build his own small contracting business.
He favours **apprenticeships** and less red tape, and leans on family before government.
He's **calm** in slower pictures and **anxious** at AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots in 2031 would hit before his **business** is ready.
whatWouldHelp: Less permit **red tape**, funded robot apprenticeships and cheap loans for **small firms**.
